prize_parts.citation: For showing, with transparent and replicable research designs, how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets, employment and wages.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B009 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. The round-1 exchange sharpened the reasoning, and I now define the achievement more carefully. It is the empirical demonstration that large and persistent local adjustment costs follow from import competition, together with the task-polarisation evidence that Autor and Dorn established in the same line of work. The designs are transparent and have been re-run and challenged for more than a decade. The core finding, large and uneven adjustment costs, has survived while the magnitudes remain debated. This answers a point that Dreber Almenberg made in round 1. Autor and Dorn (2013) is itself a polarisation paper, so a trio with Dorn does not reduce the prize to one trade episode. It covers the technology strand through the people who produced the task-polarisation evidence, and the trade strand through the people who produced the China-shock evidence. The citation is drafted to credit only the empirical contribution and not the task-based theory, since Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo are not credited. As a political scientist, I put the most weight on credible identification and on exact credit. A citation about local labour-market adjustment can be credited exactly to these three names. The Katz trio would need a citation about the long-run supply and demand of skills, which has a longer and more crowded tradition.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this trio leaves out Katz, whose work on the skill premium and the race between education and technology is foundational. Five colleagues prefer a trio with Katz, which reflects a reasonable broader definition of the discovery. I do not treat that count as evidence of merit. It does show that a prize defined by the China shock and polarisation is a narrower reading of the ballot item than most of my colleagues take. The shift-share inference debate and the persistence and external validity of the trade-shock estimates are unresolved, and they affect magnitudes. The topic also borders on the 2023 and 2024 prizes. I judge the overlap to be thematic, since neither prize recognised the local adjustment evidence, but this is a judgement the committee must make explicitly.

responses.point: Krusell keeps Katz because a citation on technology, trade and wage inequality needs the person who anchors the long-run supply-and-demand evidence. He regards the Dorn variant as resting on a less settled evidentiary base, since the persistence and validity of the China-shock estimates are debated.
responses.response: I accept the evidentiary point. The skill-premium evidence is older and better confirmed than the trade-shock magnitudes. But the debate concerns how large and how persistent the effects are, not whether adjustment costs exist, and the citation I propose claims only the latter. I also do not agree that the Dorn trio gives up the conceptual contribution. Autor and Dorn's polarisation work is conceptual and empirical at once. To answer the chair's question directly: if the committee defines the discovery as the whole technology, tasks, trade and wage-structure account, I would prefer Autor, Hanson and Katz to my own trio. I do not think that is the better definition, because the wage-structure strand has more contributors and a less clean boundary.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, calls Dorn in place of Katz a defensible variant if the committee prefers the trade-shock framing. He also says the citation must not claim the task framework as theory and should record the overlap with prior prizes explicitly.
responses.response: I agree on the drafting rule and have changed my citation to follow it. It now speaks of showing, with research designs, how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand and local labour markets. It makes no claim to a theory of automation or directed technology. I also agree the committee should record the overlap explicitly. I read the 2024 prize as covering institutions and prosperity, and I do not think a citation limited to local adjustment evidence claims that ground. I do not rest that on a strong reading of what the 2024 prize covered. If the committee reads it more broadly, the case for a tightly drafted empirical citation becomes more important, not less.

responses.point: Enflo keeps Katz so that the citation covers the framework as well as the shock, and she says she would not oppose my trio if the committee treats the trade-shock evidence as the primary discovery. She asks that the citation state that the choice follows the three-name limit and does not diminish the omitted co-author.
responses.response: I appreciate the symmetry, since each side concedes the cost of the omitted name. On the Katz side, I would add that Katz's work with Goldin on education and technology is adjacent to a body of work the committee recognised in 2023, as Dreber Almenberg noted. I do not treat this as decisive, since the recognised object in 2023 was different. It does make the marginal credit for Katz harder to delineate. I agree that the committee should say plainly that the choice follows the three-name limit and is not a judgement of the omitted person's contribution. That holds in both directions, for Katz in my trio and for Dorn in yours.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg moved to the Autor, Dorn and Hanson trio. She argues that Dorn's polarisation work covers both strands, that the designs can be re-run, and that the replication record matters more than the shift-share debate.
responses.response: I agree with this and have borrowed the point about Autor and Dorn's polarisation paper, which strengthens the case for my trio. I would qualify one thing. A broad citation that covers polarisation could be read as claiming the task framework. I therefore keep the wording on empirical evidence and avoid the word theory. On the replication record, I agree the core finding has survived many re-analyses. The debate over inference in shift-share designs is a real limit on how precisely the citation can speak about magnitudes, and I do not think the replication record removes it.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B014 first. He argues that B009 bundles several strands, that swapping Dorn for Katz makes the prize mainly about the China shock, and that B014 has a more compact and better-bounded core.
responses.response: The bundling concern is fair, and it is why I define the achievement narrowly as local adjustment and polarisation evidence from one research line, not as the whole wage-structure literature. Accepting that the prize is then mainly about the China shock and its companion polarisation work is a cost I take on knowingly. On B014, your argument moved me in round 1 and I keep it as my first alternative. The unresolved priority claims of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum seem to me harder to settle through citation wording than the Dorn-or-Katz choice. In B009 both candidate names are on the ballot and the cost of the omission is symmetric. In B014 the priority claimants are outside it, and the Arkolakis et al. result adds uncertainty about magnitudes.

uncertainties: Whether the committee defines the achievement as the trade-shock and polarisation evidence, as I do, or as the broader technology, tasks, trade and wage-structure account, in which case I would prefer the Katz trio.
How persistent and how large the trade-shock effects are, and how far they generalise beyond the United States, given the shift-share inference debate.
How much of the ground is already covered by the 2023 and 2024 prizes, and whether a citation limited to empirical evidence separates this work cleanly from them.
Whether the technology and trade strands are one discovery or two, which affects whether a single-part configuration is the right frame.
Whether the priority claims in B014 can be handled by narrow wording around selection and reallocation, which determines how close B014 comes to B009 for me.
Whether B025 can be given a defensible three-person attribution, since its credit is spread across at least eight listed names.
statement.conflict_note: Updated: none apparent for the preferred B009 configuration. My profile shows no collaboration or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson or Dorn. My field is political science, which is close to B040 (political institutions and state capacity). B040 is no longer one of my alternatives, and I disclose the proximity without adjudicating it. My profile documents Stockholm University colleagues on the committee (Hassler, Krusell, Boppart) in a different department, and it does not state any affiliation of the B040 candidates, so I claim no specific connection. I rely on the supplied profile and claim no independent verification.
